title: Cutting contests and friendly rivalry among pianists
summary: Rivalry among stride pianists was friendly, a left-hand style.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Was there a lot of rivalry and competition among those players?

Well, they would have what you would call cutting contests and they'd all show up and try to outdo each other and I suppose in this way they learned a lot of things from each other, too. This is how they passed on this -- whatever they had learned at the lesson there because the only way they could prove that they were learning anything was to be to sit down and play it. And I guess that was -- they were practicing at the same time -- at the house parties, you know, things like that, after hours.
Tell me, did that extend to rivalry on a more personal level?
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
No. No, no, I don't think so, it was a friendly kind of competition. Naturally they would try to outdo each other but there was no animosity there, you know.
Did they compete for students, too? If somebody with great potential came along, would they -- would each of them have preferred that person to become their protege.

No, I don't think so. I believe these guys, what they were studying, what they were doing was kind of hard. There just weren't that many people playing piano. That is, and taking lessons. Now there may have been a lot of piano players playing around by ear, but these guys were considered -- like Fats Waller and James P. Johnson -- they knew what they were doing.
If you'll notice on Cliff's solo there, his strength was in his left hand.
I hope that came through on the tape.
